highlights.title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
highlights.summary: It feels like Apple's Welcome Home event just happened. And the iPhone Duo announcement isn't all that far in our rearview mirror, either. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like.
body: Beyond that? There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August.

A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023. But now, in late 2026, it may finally come to fruition. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line.

This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid. It may include a few flourishes, like a magnification effect when you touch the screen or new gesture controls in native apps. But that’s it.

It’s also going to stick with the M5 series of chips for the time being — specifically, the M5 Pro and M5 Max. There might not be an M6 Pro or Max, even. Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year.

highlights.title: England suffer 15-try defeat against rampant Australia
highlights.summary: England were outclassed in a 78-0 defeat to defending champions Australia but remain in with a chance of reaching the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals.
body: Stuart Barrow's side shipped 15 tries on a unforgiving evening in Perth and must quickly regroup ahead of Friday's final pool match against Samoa, where the winner will advance to the last four.

England had no answer to a rampant Jillaroos, who dominated from the first whistle and kept a clean sheet for the second successive game. But they will be frustrated by the manner in which they gifted Australia territory and scoring opportunities during an error-strewn and ill-disciplined first half.

England's start was disastrous. They were caught offside from the kick-off and duly punished as Jaime Chapman opened the scoring, and another botched restart followed as Jenna Foubister kicked the ball straight into touch.

Australia aren't a side who require such easy access into the opposition half and they cut loose, scoring seven tries in a one-sided first half where their one negative was a suspected broken wrist suffered by Julia Robinson.

highlights.title: Xbox's First-Ever COO Is Already Leaving After A Few Months
highlights.summary: Just a couple of months after being instated as Xbox's first-ever Chief Operating Officer, Helen Chiang has left the company. Her departure reinforces just how much of a whirlwind year 2026 has been for Xbox leadership, as the company continually attempts to reinvent itself before the start of the…
body: In the July 2026 Resetting Xbox post announcing 3,200 layoffs, new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma also revealed that Helen Chiang, who was previously Studio Head at Minecraft's Mojang was becoming COO of Xbox. Chiang had "end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services," with Sharma stating that Chiang would "will bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results."

Now, just over three months after that post, The Verge reports that Helen Chiang is leaving Xbox. In a short internal memo to Xbox developers, Sharma confirmed Chiang's departure, stating that she's "grateful for her years of service" and that Xbox will "share more on COO leadership as plans are finalized." Publicly, Xbox did not highlight her departure in the same way the spotlighted Phil Spencer's, with VP of Communications Kari Perez telling The Verge that "We don't discuss individual personal matters," and "We're grateful for Helen's years of service and wish her the best."

highlights.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
highlights.summary: OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content "without risk of affecting…
body: OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.

Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.

OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”

body: England had looked set to bounce back from an 87-run hammering by Pakistan as Harry Brook's record-breaking 202 saw Sri Lanka set a massive 430 to win their match on Thursday, only for them to pull off a remarkable run chase on the penultimate ball.

The two-wicket defeat means England arrive in Lahore knowing they must beat both Pakistan on Sunday and then Sri Lanka on Thursday to give themselves a chance of of reaching the final on Saturday, October 31.

Jacks pointed out that England were faced with a similar predicament en route to winning the 2019 World Cup and, looking ahead to 2027 edition in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, he views this next week as important preparation.
"It's my first tri-series and it replicates World Cup-style pressure." Jacks told the Press Association on Friday. "You can't replicate that in training or a bilateral series.

highlights.summary: A content creator who claims to have served on a BioWare community council has shared alleged details about the cancelled next Mass Effect game, titled Mass Effect Universe.
body: In a lengthy Twitter/X post (thanks, PC Gamer ), YouTuber Dantics claimed the cancelled game was set more than 600 years after the Reaper War.
He said he'd had access via his role on the "Mass Effect Council" and had seen firsthand what BioWare was developing, and provided feedback during development.

According to Dantics, the game would have centred on a "galactic Cold War" between three major factions, rather than another Reaper-style invasion. Humanity, the Krogan, the Batarians, and others would have allied, with the Council races forming their own alliance and the Geth emerging as a third superpower.
He also mentioned Geth-built megastructures, connections between the Milky Way and Andromeda, and a "shadowy adversary".

highlights.title: Supercell hit by cyberattack, but says no player data was affected
highlights.summary: The Clash of Clans developer says it was the target of multiple attacks last week and has notified police and regulators.
body: Supercell has confirmed that an unauthorised party has accessed a platform Supercell used to host company meetings and presentations.

In an announcement on October 21, the Clash of Clans developer said it was targeted by multiple cyberattacks last week, one of which caused the incident. Based on its investigations so far, Supercell believes no player data was affected.

It says it blocked further access, took the service offline and began investigating the platform and its security experts. It has since filed a police report, submitted a notification under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, and notified the Data Protection Ombudsman, but said that because the investigation is ongoing, it cannot share further details at this time.

The videos include current and former employees, as well as some guests and partners who took part in internal events. They may contain people’s names, images and voices, and the names and email addresses of the platform’s users were also accessed.

highlights.title: My mother donated her body to science. I really wasn’t prepared for what came next
highlights.summary: The process included a gala featuring medical students doing aerial yoga and singing Taylor Swift to donors’ families. In some way, it was absolutely perfect. When my mother, Erin O’Connell, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive cancer in late 2022, one of her first thoughts was: “What will I do…
body: At the time, she was 62 years old and working as a physical therapist in Portland, Oregon, where she had recently moved to live closer to me and my family. Reluctantly, she filed for short-term disability from her job and paused her training to become a volunteer search and rescue EMT.

My mom was 40 when she started physical therapy school. I was already a teenager. Despite her newfound stress, I remember how deeply it affected me to watch her fall in love with her work. The year she took anatomy lab she told my sister and me – and anyone who would listen – that dissecting a real human body was the coolest thing she had ever gotten to do, and when she died, she wanted to donate her body to science, too.
I spent so much of my childhood wanting nothing more than my mother’s hard-earned approval, and here she was, utterly devoted to a dead body. On some level, I was jealous of that cadaver.

highlights.summary: In Compton Lecture, the distinguished legal scholar warns of potential “loss of the Enlightenment” while suggesting ways innovations can meet our civic and cultural needs.

Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance.

“It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more.

highlights.title: Russo hits winner as Arsenal end winless run at Spurs
highlights.summary: Arsenal ended their five-game winless run in the Women's Super League with a 2-1 north London derby victory over Tottenham, easing pressure on head coach Renée Slegers.
body: The Gunners had won only once in their opening six league games and started the weekend eighth, six points behind fourth-placed Spurs. They fell behind to Cathinka Tandberg's 13th-minute header but Georgia Stanway equalised four minutes later before Alessia Russo converted a second-half penalty.

Tottenham started brightly and exposed Arsenal's defensive weaknesses in transition, but their intensity faded as the first half progressed. Russo was denied by an outstanding Lize Kop save after the break before scoring from the spot in the 56th minute, after the ball struck substitute Ella Morris' outstretched hand during a scramble from a corner.
The penalty decision was a harsh one but Russo, who has missed some big chances in recent games, made no mistake to give Arsenal the lead.

Spurs pushed for an equaliser, with Shekiera Martinez having the ball in the net from close range in the 82nd minute, only for the offside flag to deny them. Arsenal held on for a much-needed win, offering some breathing room after a dismal start.
points: Arsenal ended their five-game winless run in the Women's Super League with a 2-1 north London derby victory over Tottenham, easing pressure on head coach Renée Slegers.

highlights.summary: What was the last thing you did that took 16 years to accomplish? No shame — but director Travis Knight has a different level of persistence than most of us.
body: It took Knight and his stop-motion animation studio Laika nearly two decades to bring Wildwood, their latest film, to life. Even then, the studio behind Coraline wasn't entirely prepared for the challenges of its most ambitious movie yet. Knight (who yes, also directed an entire He-Man movie over the course of this journey) says the dark fantasy pushed his team to invent new technologies, rethink old techniques, and take the kinds of risks Hollywood studios tend to avoid.

Polygon spoke with Knight about the long road to Wildwood, the film's surprisingly complicated animated feats, and why he took a unique road to theaters despite years of working with the major studios.

highlights.title: Bill Murray Is Generally OK Giving You a “Bill Murray Moment”
highlights.summary: "If you're living correctly, it's not a burden," Murray tells The Hollywood Reporter ahead of his and Tom Coyne's new Paramount golf/travel series.
body: A Course Called Ireland, an adaptation of Coyne’s 2009 book of the same name, premieres Sunday on Paramount+. The six-episode, 30-minutes-per-episode series is as breezy as the Irish coast’s weather. Its original intention was to retrace the journey chronicled in Coyne’s bestseller — the golf writer once walked the island playing every golf course it had to offer — but this version of A Course Called Ireland became, as Murray grumpily laments in at least one episode to a director, “The Bill Murray Fucking Show.”
Murray has time for pretty much everyone who wants a photo — it is the production crew taking the professional videos he’d like to avert the lenses of.

“I’m heavy in the show. For an executive producer, that’s about as heavy as you can get,” Murray told The Hollywood Reporter. “I don’t want to complain about that. I did my complaining then. It’s too late to complain.”

I’m on a Zoom call with Murray, who is wandering the streets of Boston solo after sunset, and Coyne, who is sitting in a house in the Carribean. In a bucket hat and without a care in the world, Murray speaks kindly but candidly about making his buddy Coyne’s TV dream come true.

highlights.title: Lee Chang Dong ponders the ethics of the camera
highlights.summary: Lee Chang Dong's seventh feature film, Possible Love, is inspired by true events from 2009, when a Korean conglomerate fired a third of its staff - 2,600 employees - after which many died by suicide.
body: In Possible Love, the director of Burning tackles labor struggle, human connection, and the nature of capturing others on film.

A different kind of movie would have captured the heat of that labor struggle. Possible Love picks up with the characters in the aftermath, a murkier time that defies easy understanding. The film opens with an epigraph: “Thou shall not covet.” What follows is a movie about characters who covet. They covet each other’s job, designer clothes, spouses, and positionality. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-Yeon) is the long-suffering wife of Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), her laid-off husband. At a funeral of a colleague who died by suicide, Mi-ok and Ho-seok meet another couple, documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her rich husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). And off we go.

The Verge spoke with Lee during his trip to New York about how he arrived at his politics, porousness between people, the properties of the camera, and what it is like to work with Netflix. The interview was conducted in Korean and translated into English.
I am also from Daegu. I wonder how this fact shaped you? And more broadly, to whom or what do you owe your political education?
points: Lee Chang Dong's seventh feature film, Possible Love, is inspired by true events from 2009, when a Korean conglomerate fired a third of its staff - 2,600 employees - after which many died by suicide.
In Possible Love, the director of Burning tackles labor struggle, human connection, and the nature of capturing others on film.
A different kind of movie would have captured the heat of that labor struggle.

highlights.title: Aaron Paul Originally Had A Much More Important Role In Clayface
highlights.summary: Clayface hit theaters this weekend, but one actor's role turned out to be smaller than expected. We knew Aaron Paul would be in the DC horror flick prior to its release, but in the final film, he cameos in just one scene.
body: Breaking Bad and Dispatch actor Aaron Paul appears during one of Clayface's most memorable sequences, as Matt Hagen transforms into him during a sequence set in Vesuvius to kill a Szabo gang member who killed his father. It turns out Aaron Paul was portraying Matt Hagen's abusive father, with Watkins telling Entertainment Weekly that Paul's character originally had more scenes in the movie.

"In terms of trying to figure out the character, it was, 'How much is Matt defined by his past, and how much is he an everyman?' At one point, we were looking at it and thinking, 'Is it the sins of the father?' But actually, as we worked on the script, I thought that notion of revenge was more universal and more relatable to all of us," Watkins revealed, highlighting how the central themes of the movie evolved in post-production.

"It doesn’t matter whether you’re carrying a trauma or any of that," he continued. "If we’re slighted, we carry this sense of being wronged, and we all want to do something, but generally in life we can’t do anything about it, and we’re powerless."

highlights.title: Nintendo Is Still Being Wildly Underestimated
highlights.summary: Switchboard is Polygon's weekly newsletter for all things Nintendo, sent on Thursdays and published on the site on Saturdays. You can subscribe here.
body: Nintendo has always enjoyed the respect of critics. The games, at their best, are just too good for things to be otherwise. It is total critical orthodoxy that Shigeru Miyamoto is one of the greatest and most influential game designers of all time, and that Mario and Zelda games are foundational texts of the video game medium that have successfully rewritten themselves and stayed relevant over time.

Yet there have been times throughout the company's history when Nintendo's image, and the audiences it has chosen to cultivate, have deflated this reputation. In the edgy late 1990s and early 2000s, when PlayStation ruled all, the family-friendliness and colorful styling of Nintendo games led to some people writing them off as kids' stuff. And when Nintendo sought out a new casual-gaming audience with the Wii and DS, some of its core fans felt betrayed, and couldn't find the depth or sophistication they wanted in the games.

highlights.title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
highlights.summary: Security researchers used AI tools to help uncover years-old vulnerabilities in the PHP web scripting language. Then the AI-assisted attacks began.
body: As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.
So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

highlights.title: I Asked 8 Chefs to Name the Best Jarred Pasta Sauce — This Is the One They Swear By
highlights.summary: Pasta is one of my favorite foods, and what really makes it is the sauce. A good sauce can often require simmering the ingredients for hours until all the flavors have melded. But sometimes we don’t have time for that.
body: So when we need something simple, quick, and easy to grab, jarred sauces can be a kitchen hero. I’ve tried many on the market, but was curious to learn which ones professional chefs give the stamp of approval. So I asked 8 chefs: What is the best jarred marinara sauce? One clearly swept the board but there were a few other favorites. Here are the jarred sauces you should stock your pantry shelves with.

The majority of the chefs (6 out of 8!) chose Rao’s Homemade as their top pick, praising it for being a great base for dishes like chicken Parmesan, lasagna, pasta puttanesca, and more. (It is Ina Garten’s favorite, too.) Jamie Milne, cookbook author of Everything Delish and busy mom of two, loves how close to homemade it tastes. “Rao’s has that rich, slow-simmered tomato flavor that you would expect from a sauce that’s been cooking on the stove for hours,” Milne said. “It’s made with simple ingredients like Italian tomatoes, olive oil, garlic, onions, and herbs, and you can really taste the difference.”
